messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard deviation of the sampling distribution (standard error)**  

For a one‑sided or two‑sided *t*–test you need the **standard error of the mean**, which is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \(\bar X\):

\[
\sigma_{\bar{X}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
\(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
\(n = 40\) (number of observations)

---

### Calculation

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{\bar{X}} &= \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}\\[4pt]
&= \frac{1.4}{6.32455532}\\[4pt]
&\approx 0.2215 .
\end{aligned}
\]

So the **standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test statistic** (i.e., the standard error of the mean) is approximately:

\[
\boxed{\sigma_{\bar{X}}\;\approx\;0.222}
\]

*(Rounded to three decimal places.)*

If you were asked for something else—e.g., the variance of the test statistic—it would simply be \( (\sigma_{\bar{X}})^2 \approx 0.049.\)*
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" given sample mean=98.2, std dev=1.4, n=40, population mean=98.6.

They likely want the standard error (SE) used in t-test? Standard deviation of sampling distribution under H0: sqrt(s^2/n). So SE = s / sqrt(n) = 1.4/sqrt(40).

Compute sqrt(40)=~6.3249; 1.4/6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. They might also ask for standard deviation of null hypothesis test statistic? That would be same as SE because t-statistic uses this SD. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of means under null: sigma_xbar = sigma_pop / sqrt(n), but we use sample sd estimate. So answer ~0.22.

Thus respond accordingly. Also mention formula. Provide numeric result.
